title: Investing basics
examples: What is the difference between buying shares and buying bonds?
How does spreading investments help reduce risk?
Can I invest in something without understanding it first?

explain.say: Today we will learn about basic investing ideas. We will look at shares, bonds, and funds.
A share means you own a tiny part of a company. If the company does well, your share value might rise.

draw.text: Shares: Own a part of a company

explain.say: A bond is like lending money to a government or a company. They promise to pay you back with interest.
A fund pools money from many people to buy many different investments together. This is managed by a professional.

draw.text: Funds: Pool money for many investments

explain.say: If you only put all your money in one place, you take on high risk. This is called concentration risk.

draw.text: Risk: Putting all money in one place

explain.say: Diversification means spreading your investments across different areas. This helps manage overall risk.

faq.q: What is the main difference between shares and bonds?
faq.a: Shares mean ownership in a company, while bonds mean you are lending money to an entity. Shares can grow more but are riskier than bonds.
asks: Does a bond mean I am a lender?

faq.q: Why is diversification important when I start investing?
faq.a: Diversification helps reduce your risk because if one investment performs poorly, others might perform well. It smooths out your overall returns.
asks: What is the purpose of spreading risk?
Does diversification mean I cannot make much money?

faq.q: Are funds always better than buying things myself?
faq.a: Funds are convenient because a professional manages the buying and selling for you. However, you must still understand the underlying assets.
asks: Should I use a fund always?
What is the benefit of using a fund?

faq.q: What is 'risk' in the context of investing?
faq.a: Risk is the chance that your investment might lose some or all of its value. Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk.
asks: How do I measure investment risk?

faq.q: Can I invest in things I do not understand?
faq.a: It is wise to only invest in things you have researched or that are managed by trusted professionals. Never invest money you cannot afford to lose.
asks: Do I need to know everything to invest?
What is the safest way to invest?

facts: Shares represent fractional ownership in a corporation.
Bonds are debt instruments where the issuer pays interest over time.
Funds combine money from many investors to buy a diverse portfolio.
Diversification spreads risk across different asset types.

quiz.say: If you buy shares in a technology company, you are:
quiz.show: Own a piece of the company.

options.show: Taking out a loan from the bank.
options.say: Taking out a loan from the bank.

options.show: Buying a basket of many stocks.
options.say: Buying a basket of many stocks.

quiz.why: Shares give you a direct stake, meaning you own a part of the company's profits and assets.

wrong.0: This is a banking transaction, not an investment in a company.
wrong.2: That describes buying a bond, which is debt, not ownership.
wrong.3: That describes a fund, which pools many different assets together.

quiz.say: What is the primary benefit of diversification?
quiz.why: By not putting all your eggs in one basket, a dip in one area is balanced by stability in another.

wrong.1: No investment can guarantee high returns; risk always exists.
wrong.2: Nothing in investing is completely risk-free.
wrong.3: You still need to research the types of assets you are buying.

quiz.say: If you buy a bond, what is the issuer promising to do?

options.show: Repay the loan with interest payments.
options.say: Repay the loan with interest payments.

options.show: Allowing you to vote on company decisions.
options.say: Allowing you to vote on company decisions.

options.show: Making you a partner in the business.
options.say: Making you a partner in the business.

quiz.why: Bonds are contracts where the issuer promises to pay you back the original amount plus regular interest payments.

wrong.1: Bonds pay fixed interest, but their principal value can still change.
wrong.2: Voting rights are usually associated with owning shares, not bonds.
wrong.3: A bondholder is a lender, not a partner or owner.
